lessonTitle: Antimicrobial Stewardship: De-escalation and the Cost of Broad-Spectrum Therapy

blocks.text: On day three of a ward round, a patient who was admitted septic and started on a very broad intravenous antibiotic is afebrile and eating. The urine culture has grown a single organism with a narrow susceptibility pattern. The antibiotic chart still shows the original drug, unchanged, with no stop date. What the team does next decides whether this patient, and the ward, face avoidable harm.

blocks.markdown: Every antibiotic course exerts **selection pressure**: it removes susceptible bacteria and favours resistant ones, in the patient's own flora as well as in the infecting organism. **Antimicrobial stewardship** is the coordinated set of interventions that make sure each patient gets an antimicrobial only when needed, and then the right one, for the right duration, to improve outcomes while limiting resistance, adverse effects and cost.

blocks.title: Antimicrobial stewardship
blocks.text: A multidisciplinary programme (prescribers, microbiologists, pharmacists, nurses) that promotes appropriate use of antimicrobials: right drug, right dose, right route, right duration, started promptly when indicated and reviewed regularly.

items: Treat only when there is clinical evidence of bacterial infection; do not treat colonisation or viral illness.
Take appropriate cultures before starting antibiotics, where this causes no delay.
Start promptly in serious infection, guided by local guidelines and local resistance patterns.
Document the indication, drug, dose, route and an intended review or stop date.
Review at 48-72 hours with the results in hand: continue, stop, narrow (de-escalate), or switch from intravenous to oral.
Use the narrowest effective spectrum and the shortest effective duration.
Audit prescribing and feed results back to prescribers.

blocks.markdown: **De-escalation and culture-guided therapy.** Empirical therapy is deliberately broad because the organism is unknown. Once culture and sensitivity results identify the organism and show which drugs it is susceptible to, therapy should be **narrowed to the most targeted effective agent**, switched to oral if the patient is well and absorbing, or **stopped** if infection is excluded. This works for three reasons: it removes unnecessary pressure on the patient's normal flora, which lowers the risk of resistance and of superinfection; it reduces toxicity and cost; and a narrow agent is frequently equal or better (for example, a narrow penicillin is often more effective against a susceptible organism than a broad agent).

blocks.title: De-escalating on a culture result
blocks.prompt: A patient started on a broad-spectrum carbapenem for sepsis from an unknown source has blood cultures that grow Escherichia coli, susceptible to amoxicillin and several narrower agents at 48 hours. The patient is afebrile and eating. What is the stewardship decision, and what is the reasoning?

steps.text: Identify what changed: the organism and its susceptibilities are now known, and the patient has improved clinically.
Choose a narrower effective drug from the susceptibility report that suits the source; consider switching from intravenous to oral since the patient is well.
Set a review date and a total duration appropriate for the infection.
Explain the benefit: less selection pressure on gut flora (lower risk of resistant organisms and Clostridioides difficile infection) and lower toxicity.

blocks.answer: De-escalate to a narrow-spectrum, susceptible agent, ideally oral, with a defined stop date.

blocks.markdown: **Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI).** *C. difficile* is a Gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobic bacillus. The normal colonic flora provides **colonisation resistance**. Broad-spectrum antibiotics deplete this flora, allowing *C. difficile* spores, which are acquired in hospital or the community and survive alcohol hand gel, to germinate and multiply. The organism releases **toxin A** (an enterotoxin) and **toxin B** (a cytotoxin), which damage colonic epithelium and cause watery diarrhoea, colitis, and in severe cases pseudomembranous colitis, toxic megacolon and perforation. Antibiotics with the strongest association include clindamycin, cephalosporins (especially later-generation), fluoroquinolones and broad penicillins, but any antibiotic can precipitate CDI. Other risk factors are advanced age, hospital stay, proton pump inhibitor use and immunosuppression. Diagnosis rests on stool testing for toxin or toxin genes in a patient with diarrhoea. Management principles include stopping or narrowing the inciting antibiotic where possible, using a CDI-directed agent, and infection control with soap-and-water handwashing and contact precautions.

blocks.caption: Stewardship actions and the problems they address
rows: Therapy cannot be targeted; culture yield falls
Treat as long as necessary and no longer

blocks.caption: A common stewardship metric: each day on each antibiotic counts as one day of therapy

blocks.title: Calculating a stewardship metric
blocks.prompt: A ward records 560 antibiotic days of therapy over 4 000 patient-days. What is the DOT per 1000 patient-days?

steps.text: Divide days of therapy by patient-days: 560 / 4000 = 0.14.

blocks.answer: 140 days of therapy per 1000 patient-days; a falling trend after intervention suggests reduced exposure.

blocks.title: De-escalation is evidence-led
blocks.text: Culture and sensitivity results are the evidence that allows safe narrowing. Without them clinicians tend to keep broad therapy running, which increases resistance selection and CDI risk.

blocks.title: Stewardship is not under-treatment
blocks.text: In suspected sepsis, prompt effective empirical therapy must not be delayed. Stewardship is about review and rationalisation, not withholding antibiotics from patients who need them. Also, CDI can occur with any antibiotic and may appear weeks after the course ends.

points: Stewardship ensures the right drug, dose, route and duration, with review.
Culture and sensitivity results allow narrowing, oral switch or stopping, reducing selection pressure and harm.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt colonisation resistance and predispose to C. difficile infection (toxins A and B).
Metrics such as days of therapy per 1000 patient-days support audit.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the aim of antimicrobial stewardship?

options.text: Optimise antimicrobial use so patients get the right drug, dose, route and duration while limiting resistance and harm
Restrict all antibiotics to reduce cost
Use the broadest available drug in every infection

questions.correctOptionText: Optimise antimicrobial use so patients get the right drug, dose, route and duration while limiting resistance and harm

distractorRationale.b: Stewardship is about appropriateness, not blanket restriction.
distractorRationale.c: Broadest drugs drive resistance and CDI.
distractorRationale.d: Fixed 24-hour stops are not a stewardship principle.

questions.explanation: Stewardship aims for effective treatment with minimal harm. It requires review and individualised duration rather than blanket rules.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with leg cellulitis is started on a broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic. At 72 hours blood and wound cultures grow Streptococcus pyogenes susceptible to benzylpenicillin and amoxicillin. He is afebrile and eating. What is the best stewardship step?

options.text: Narrow to a susceptible narrow-spectrum agent, consider an oral switch, and set a stop date
Continue the broad agent unchanged in case another organism is present
Stop all treatment immediately without review

questions.correctOptionText: Narrow to a susceptible narrow-spectrum agent, consider an oral switch, and set a stop date

distractorRationale.b: Unnecessary breadth increases resistance and CDI risk.
distractorRationale.c: Escalation is not justified in an improving patient with a defined organism.
distractorRationale.d: Stopping without review is unsafe in an active infection.

questions.explanation: The culture has identified a susceptible organism and the patient is improving, so narrowing is safe and reduces harm. A review date prevents unlimited courses.

questions.stem: Why do broad-spectrum antibiotics predispose to Clostridioides difficile infection?

options.text: They deplete normal colonic flora, removing colonisation resistance so C. difficile can multiply and produce toxins
They convert C. difficile into a toxin-producing strain by transformation
They directly damage colonic epithelium via lipopolysaccharide

questions.correctOptionText: They deplete normal colonic flora, removing colonisation resistance so C. difficile can multiply and produce toxins

distractorRationale.b: Antibiotics do not create toxin production this way.
distractorRationale.c: Spores resist most antibiotics and survive.
distractorRationale.d: C. difficile is Gram-positive and has no LPS; damage is by toxins A and B.

questions.explanation: The normal flora normally prevent C. difficile from establishing. When antibiotics deplete it, spores germinate and vegetative cells release toxins A and B that injure the colonic mucosa.

questions.stem: Which is a feature of C. difficile that helps it persist in hospital environments?

options.text: Spores that survive alcohol hand gel

questions.correctOptionText: Spores that survive alcohol hand gel

distractorRationale.b: Capsule is not the main persistence feature.
distractorRationale.c: C. difficile is extracellular in the gut lumen.
distractorRationale.d: It is Gram-positive and lacks an outer membrane.

questions.explanation: Spores resist drying, heat and alcohol, so soap-and-water handwashing and environmental cleaning are needed. This is why infection control is part of CDI management.

questions.stem: True or false: In a clinically improving patient, a blood culture result showing a susceptible organism should prompt review for narrowing or stopping broad-spectrum therapy.
questions.explanation: Culture and sensitivity results are the evidence that justifies de-escalation. Narrowing reduces selection pressure and the risk of superinfection such as C. difficile.

questions.stem: A medical ward records 735 antibiotic days of therapy over 3 500 patient-days. Calculate the days of therapy per 1000 patient-days.
questions.explanation: DOT per 1000 patient-days = 735 / 3500 x 1000 = 210. Auditing this metric over time shows whether stewardship interventions reduce antibiotic exposure.

questions.stem: A hospital reports 27 cases of hospital-onset C. difficile infection over 18 000 occupied bed-days. Calculate the incidence in cases per 10 000 bed-days.
questions.explanation: Incidence = 27 / 18 000 x 10 000 = 15 per 10 000 bed-days. Tracking this rate alongside antibiotic use shows whether stewardship reduces CDI.

questions.stem: State the core principles of antimicrobial stewardship that a prescriber applies when starting and reviewing an antibiotic.
markingGuide: Treat only when bacterial infection is likely; avoid treating viral illness or colonisation
Take cultures before antibiotics where no delay results
Choose according to local guidelines and likely organisms; start promptly in serious infection
Document indication, dose, route and intended review or stop date
Review at 48-72 hours: continue, narrow, switch to oral, or stop
Use the narrowest effective spectrum and shortest effective duration
questions.explanation: These principles summarise the right drug, dose, route and duration approach. Documented review is what makes de-escalation happen in practice.

questions.stem: Explain why culture and sensitivity results should guide de-escalation of empirical therapy, and give two benefits for the patient and the wider hospital.
markingGuide: Empirical therapy is broad because the organism is unknown
Culture identifies the organism and sensitivity shows effective narrow options
Narrowing reduces selection pressure on normal flora and lowers resistance
Reduces risk of C. difficile infection and adverse effects
Lower cost and possible oral switch or earlier stop
questions.explanation: Results turn a guess into a targeted treatment. The patient benefits from less toxicity and less flora disruption, and the hospital from reduced resistance pressure.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman develops profuse watery diarrhoea five days after finishing a course of a broad-spectrum cephalosporin for a chest infection. Stool tests detect C. difficile toxin. Explain the pathogenesis of her illness and the infection-control implications.
markingGuide: Antibiotic depleted normal colonic flora, losing colonisation resistance
C. difficile spores germinate and multiply
Toxins A (enterotoxin) and B (cytotoxin) damage colonic epithelium causing diarrhoea and colitis
Risk factors: age, hospitalisation, broad-spectrum antibiotic
Spores survive alcohol gel so soap-and-water hand hygiene, contact precautions and environmental cleaning are needed
questions.explanation: CDI results from loss of protective flora followed by toxin production. Because spores are hardy, infection control differs from many other organisms.
